prompt: Which of these creatures is NOT an insect?
hint: Insects have six legs, but spiders have eight!

fact.text: Spiders and tarantulas are arachnids with eight legs, while every true insect has six legs!
fact.support: Garden spiders are eight-legged arachnids, whereas all true insects have six legs.

misconception: Thinking spiders are insects because both are tiny creepy-crawlies with many legs.

prompt: Which of these wild meadow wonders is NOT a plant?
hint: Mushrooms are fungi, so they cannot make their own food from sunlight.

fact.text: Mushrooms are fungi with a stem and cap, which cannot make food from sunlight like green plants do!
fact.support: Mushrooms are fungi that absorb nutrients from wood, while plants create food with sunlight.

misconception: Thinking mushrooms are plants because they grow in forest dirt and have stems.

prompt: Tap all the animals that lay eggs in nests or soil!
hint: Look for the turtle with a shell and the soaring eagle.

fact.text: Female turtles bury their eggs in sand or soil to hatch in warmth!
fact.support: Mother turtles bury their eggs in sandy soil so their babies can hatch.

misconception: Thinking all furry land animals lay eggs like birds and reptiles do.

prompt: Tap all the creatures that can fly!
hint: Butterflies, bees, and even furry bats have wings for flying!

fact.text: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly; flying squirrels only glide.
fact.support: Bats have winged hands that flap, making them the only mammals capable of true flight.

misconception: Thinking flying squirrels fly with wings instead of just gliding through the air.

prompt: Order the stages of this winged insect's life cycle from start!
hint: Start from egg, hatch to caterpillar, form chrysalis, then emerge flying.

fact.text: Butterflies go through complete metamorphosis in four stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, and adult!
fact.support: An insect begins as a tiny egg, hatches into a caterpillar, rests in a chrysalis, and emerges as a butterfly.

misconception: Thinking caterpillars turn straight into flying butterflies without resting inside a chrysalis.

prompt: Order how a little plant grows up into a lovely bloom!
hint: Begin with the seed in soil and finish with the bloom.

fact.text: When a seed germinates, a root sprouts downward first, followed by a green shoot growing upward toward the light!
fact.support: A planted seed germinates in soil, pushes out a tiny sprout, grows a green stem, and opens into a sunflower.

misconception: Thinking leaves and flowers bloom before a seed grows roots into the soil.

prompt: Which planet is the hottest planet in our solar system?
hint: Mercury is closest, but Venus traps extreme heat under thick clouds.

fact.text: Venus is the hottest planet in our solar system because its atmosphere traps heat!
fact.support: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps intense solar heat.

misconception: Thinking Mercury is the hottest planet just because it is closest to the Sun.

prompt: What kind of space object is our warm daytime Sun?
hint: The Sun is not a planet: it is our nearest star.

fact.text: The light of daytime on Earth comes from our closest star, the Sun!
fact.support: Our daytime Sun is a giant glowing ball of hot plasma, which is a star.

misconception: Thinking the Sun is a gigantic planet because it looks big and round in our daytime sky.

prompt: Tap all the objects that produce their own glowing light!
hint: The Moon does not make light: it reflects light from the Sun!

fact.text: The Moon does not make light; it simply reflects light from the Sun!
fact.support: The Moon produces no light itself; moonlight is sunlight reflecting off its dusty surface.

misconception: Thinking the Moon makes its own light like a glowing lightbulb in the night sky.

prompt: Tap all the giant planets that have rings around them!
hint: Saturn has famous rings, but Jupiter and Uranus have rings too!

fact.text: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune all have rings circling around them in space!
fact.support: Saturn has the most visible rings, but Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune also have ring systems.

misconception: Thinking Saturn is the only planet in our solar system that has rings.

prompt: Order the first four rocky planets starting closest to Sun!
hint: Start at Mercury, then Venus, our Earth, and red planet Mars.

fact.text: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are inner rocky planets made of dense metals and stone!
fact.support: Mercury is closest to the Sun, followed by Venus, Earth, and Mars in orbital order.

misconception: Thinking Earth is closer to the Sun than Venus because summer feels so warm.

prompt: Order these space neighbors from closest to Earth to furthest!
hint: The Moon orbits Earth, Sun is next, distant stars are furthest.

fact.text: The Moon is about 239,000 miles from Earth. The Sun, our closest star, is about 93 million miles away.
fact.support: The Moon orbits Earth at 238,855 miles away, the Sun is 93 million miles away, and distant stars are 25 trillion miles.

misconception: Thinking stars at night are closer to us than the Moon because they twinkle so brightly.

prompt: Who has more bones inside their skeleton?
hint: Babies start with about 300 bones that fuse together over time!

fact.text: A newborn baby starts with around 300 bones, which fuse into 206 bones in an adult person!
fact.support: Human babies are born with around 300 bones, which gradually fuse into 206 adult bones.

misconception: Thinking bigger adults must have more bones in their skeletons than tiny babies.

prompt: Which is the LARGEST single organ of the human body?
hint: It covers your body from your head all the way to your toes!

fact.text: Skin is the largest organ of the human body, protecting everything inside your body.
fact.support: Skin is the human body's largest organ, forming an outer shield that protects internal parts.

misconception: Thinking skin is just thin wrapping rather than the largest organ of the human body.

prompt: Which is the hardest part of your body?
hint: It forms the tough gleaming shield covering every tooth in your mouth!

fact.text: Tooth enamel is the hardest part of your body, protecting each tooth with a hard mineral shield.
fact.support: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body, even tougher than skeleton bones.

misconception: Thinking thick leg bones are the hardest material in the human body.

prompt: Tap all the sensory parts found on your smiling face!
hint: Knees bend for running, but eyes, nose, and tongue explore senses!

fact.text: The tongue has taste buds that detect sweet, salty, sour, savory and bitter tastes!
fact.support: Your tongue has thousands of tiny taste buds that send flavor signals directly to your brain.

misconception: Thinking you taste food with your teeth and lips instead of taste buds on your tongue.

prompt: Order by teeth, fewest to most!
hint: Babies start with zero teeth, toddlers grow twenty baby teeth, and adults have up to thirty-two!

fact.text: Babies usually start with zero teeth, toddlers get 20 baby teeth, and adults can grow up to 32 permanent teeth!
fact.support: Infants start with zero teeth, toddlers grow 20 baby teeth, and adults can have 32 permanent teeth.

misconception: Thinking babies are born with a full set of teeth already in their mouths.

prompt: Order what happens as healthy food journeys through your body!
hint: Teeth chew first, throat swallows, and stomach digests into energy.

fact.text: Your teeth chew meals, which travel through the esophagus into the stomach for digestion!
fact.support: Teeth chew food, the throat swallows it down the esophagus, and the stomach digests it.

misconception: Thinking food drops directly into the stomach without being chewed by teeth first.

prompt: Which creature constructs wooden dams to create safe family ponds?
hint: Beavers gnaw trees with orange teeth to build sturdy lodges and dams.
misconception: Thinking beavers build dams just to store food rather than create deep protective ponds.

fact.text: Beavers build wooden dams that form slow-moving ponds, creating rich wetland homes for many wild species!
fact.support: By building dams that form ponds, beavers provide wetlands and resources for dozens of wildlife species.

prompt: Tap the wetland habitats where wild American alligators live!
hint: Alligators thrive in freshwater swamps, marshes, and riverbanks.
misconception: Thinking alligators live in open ocean waves with salty water like dolphins.

fact.text: American alligators primarily inhabit freshwater swamps and marshes, though they also swim in rivers and lakes!
fact.support: Alligators primarily inhabit freshwater swamps and marshes, and can also live in rivers and lakes.

prompt: What woody plant makes up almost the entire diet of giant pandas?
hint: Pandas spend hours each day happily munching on stalks of bamboo.
misconception: Thinking giant pandas hunt fish or small mammals in the snow like polar bears.

fact.text: Giant pandas have strong jaws and broad teeth perfectly adapted for crushing tough bamboo stalks!
fact.support: Giant pandas have strong jaw muscles and broad molar teeth to crush tough bamboo stalks.

prompt: Which body parts join together to form an elephant's long trunk?
hint: An elephant breathes and smells through its trunk because it is an elongated nose.
misconception: Thinking an elephant's trunk is an extra giant arm or special single muscle.

fact.text: An elephant's flexible trunk is actually a wonderful fusion of its nose and upper lip!
fact.support: An elephant's trunk is anatomically a fusion of its nose and upper lip.

prompt: What causes different seasons to cycle throughout the year across our globe?
hint: Earth leans on a slant as it circles around the Sun.
misconception: Thinking summer happens because planet Earth travels closer to the Sun in July.

fact.text: Earth's tilted axis creates our seasons because different regions receive direct solar rays throughout the year!
fact.support: Earth's tilted axis creates the different seasons as our planet orbits around the Sun.

prompt: Why does our daytime meadow sky appear brightly colored in blue?
hint: Blue light waves scatter in all directions through the gases in our atmosphere.
misconception: Thinking the clear blue sky is just reflecting blue water from the world's oceans.

fact.text: Sunlight contains all colors, but blue light is scattered more across our atmosphere than other colors!
fact.support: Blue light waves scatter more across the atmosphere than other colors because they are shorter.

prompt: Tap the planets that are gas giants without a solid surface!
hint: Jupiter and Saturn have thick clouds with no solid ground underneath.
misconception: Thinking every planet in our solar system has hard ground where you could stand.

fact.text: Jupiter and Saturn are massive gas giants that have thick atmospheres without a solid rocky ground!
fact.support: Jupiter is a gas giant planet that does not have a solid rocky surface.

prompt: What is the typical climate on the red surface of Mars?
hint: Mars is much further from the Sun than Earth, making it very chilly.
misconception: Thinking Mars is scorching hot because its rusty red rocks look like glowing flames.

fact.text: Mars is a cold desert world located much further from the warmth of the Sun!
fact.support: Mars is a cold desert world that experiences freezing temperatures across its rocky landscape.

prompt: Which tireless organ acts as a powerful automatic pump inside your chest?
hint: Your heart beats continuously day and night to power circulation throughout your body.
misconception: Thinking lungs pump the blood through your veins instead of breathing in oxygen.

fact.text: Your heart is a powerful automatic pump that beats to deliver oxygen throughout your entire body!
fact.support: The heart is a powerful automatic pump that delivers circulation throughout the human body.

prompt: Tap two essential vital signs doctors check to see how you are doing!
hint: Doctors check how your heart beats and how lungs take in breaths.
misconception: Thinking shoe size or how tall you are counted as medical vital signs.

fact.text: Vital signs reflect essential body functions, including your heartbeat rate and your regular breathing rate!
fact.support: Vital signs measure essential bodily functions including heartbeat rate and regular breathing rate.

prompt: Which breathing organs serve as the primary parts of your respiratory system?
hint: Your lungs take in air every time you breathe in and out.
misconception: Thinking food and air both pass into your stomach when you inhale deeply.

fact.text: Your two lungs are the primary organs of the respiratory system, taking in fresh oxygen!
fact.support: The two lungs serve as the primary organs of the human respiratory system.

prompt: Order the digestive organs as a swallowed bite travels downward through them!
hint: Food moves from your throat into the stomach, and then enters the intestines.
misconception: Thinking food drops into the intestines before reaching the acid in your stomach.

fact.text: Swallowed food travels through the digestive tract, moving from throat into stomach and intestines!
fact.support: Peristalsis moves food through the digestive tract, passing from throat into stomach and intestines.

prompt: Order how parent eagles raise a new family from start to finish!
hint: Think about what parent eagles build before laying their eggs.

fact.text: Parent eagles construct large stick nests, incubate their laid eggs, and raise hatched chicks together!
fact.support: Parent eagles construct a nest, lay eggs, and protect the hatched chick.
evidence: Eagles construct their nests near water in tall trees or on cliffs using large sticks

misconception: Children sometimes think birds find ready-made nests, but parents carefully build a nest before laying eggs.

prompt: Which of these real creatures is actually a giant living lizard?
hint: One of these scaly creatures is the world's largest living lizard.

fact.text: Komodo dragons are large lizards with long tails, strong agile necks, and sturdy limbs.
fact.support: Komodo dragons are large lizards with long tails and sturdy limbs.
evidence: Komodo dragons are large lizards with long tails, strong and agile necks, and sturdy limbs

misconception: Children often confuse dragons with make-believe fantasy beasts, but Komodo dragons are real giant lizards.

prompt: Tap all the wild animals that hunt together in coordinated teams!
hint: Two of these animals cooperate in packs or prides to find food.

fact.text: Gray wolves hunt cooperatively in packs, and African lions team up in prides to catch prey together!
fact.support: Gray wolves hunt cooperatively in packs while African lions team up in prides.
evidence: Gray wolves hunt cooperatively in packs and are able to take down prey larger than they are including caribou, moose, deer and bison

misconception: Children often believe big predators always hunt as solitary loners, but wolves and lions hunt in coordinated teams.

prompt: Which speedy sprinter has semi-retractable claws that act like running cleats?
hint: Think about which spotted sprinter needs non-slip traction to run fast.

fact.text: Special paw pads and semi-retractable claws provide cheetahs great traction while running!
fact.support: Cheetahs use special paw pads and semi-retractable claws for great traction.
evidence: Special paw pads and semi-retractable claws provide great traction

misconception: Children often think all cats retract their claws fully into paws, but cheetah claws stay out for running grip.

prompt: Order how the illuminated lunar shapes grow across the monthly night cycle!
hint: Start with the dark phase before the silver crescent appears.

fact.text: As the Moon orbits Earth each month, it shifts from new phase, to waxing crescent, to full orb!
fact.support: The cycle progresses from a new phase, to a waxing crescent, to a bright full orb.
evidence: The Moon displays these eight phases one after the other as it moves through its cycle each month

misconception: Children sometimes think the Moon physically changes shape or grows, but we just see different lighted angles.

prompt: Tap all the frozen planets known by astronomers as ice giants!
hint: The two coldest outer gas planets contain deep icy slush layers.

fact.text: Neptune and Uranus are classified as ice giants because they contain thick slushy layers of icy materials!
fact.support: Neptune, like Uranus, is classified by astronomers as an ice giant.
evidence: Neptune, like Uranus, is an ice giant

misconception: Children often classify all four outer planets simply as gas giants, but Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

prompt: Which distant planet is famous for being dark, cold, and very windy?
hint: This deep blue planet has supersonic icy storms and faint rings.

fact.text: Neptune is a very cold, windy world encircled by thin rings far away from the Sun!
fact.support: Neptune is a very cold and windy world orbiting far out in our solar system.
evidence: Neptune is a very cold, windy world

misconception: Children might think wind only blows on Earth with trees, but supersonic icy winds howl on Neptune.

prompt: Tap all the inner worlds classified by scientists as terrestrial planets!
hint: Select the two rocky worlds with solid ground underfoot.

fact.text: Mercury and Earth are terrestrial planets with compact rocky crusts beneath our boots!
fact.support: Mercury is a terrestrial planet with a solid rocky surface like Earth.

misconception: Children sometimes think all planets are made of gas like Jupiter, but inner planets are solid rock.

prompt: Tap all the types of nerve tissues found inside the human brain!
hint: Nerve tissues in the brain come in both gray and white varieties.

fact.text: The human brain contains deep white matter as well as surface gray matter to process signals!
fact.support: The human brain contains deep white matter as well as surface gray matter.
evidence: White matter is found in the deeper tissues of the brain (subcortical)

misconception: Children often imagine the brain is all one solid pink color, but it consists of distinct white and gray matter.

prompt: Which inner eye part changes shape to focus incoming light rays?
hint: This clear part behind the pupil flexes to focus your sight.

fact.text: The flexible lens inside your eye changes shape to focus light directly onto the retina!
fact.support: The flexible lens inside your eye changes shape to focus light on the retina.
evidence: The lens itself is flexible and suspended by ligaments which allow it to change shape to focus light on the retina, which is composed of sensory neurons

misconception: Children often believe eyes just project sight like flashlights, but the flexible lens focuses light onto the sensitive retina inside.

prompt: Order how fresh breaths travel deeper into your lower respiratory airway!
hint: Follow breath from the windpipe down into branching tubes and air sacs.

fact.text: The major respiratory structures include the windpipe, which branches into bronchial tubes and tiny alveoli air sacs!
fact.support: Inhaled air travels down the windpipe, splits into branching bronchi, and reaches tiny alveoli.
evidence: The major passages and structures of the lower respiratory tract include the windpipe (trachea) and within the lungs, the bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli

misconception: Children often imagine air sits in one big hollow bag, but airway passages branch into millions of microscopic sacs.

prompt: Tap all the vital chest organs sheltered inside your curved rib cage!
hint: Your sturdy rib bones wrap around two vital chest organs.

fact.text: Your curved rib cage acts like a protective shield around your chest to shelter both your lungs and heart!
fact.support: Your rib cage forms a protective shield around your chest to protect your lungs and heart.
evidence: Your rib cage, for example, acts like a shield around your chest to protect important organs inside such as your lungs and heart

misconception: Children sometimes think ribs are just rigid sticks, but together they form an elastic protective cage shielding internal chest organs.
